name: Predicting Distress and Default
title: Predicting Distress and Default
answer: Predicting distress and default is the practice of estimating whether a borrower or issuer will fail to meet its obligations, when that failure might occur, and how much value would be lost if it does. It covers corporate bonds, loans, sovereign debt, structured credit, and consumer or small business exposures, depending on the portfolio. The work separates probability of default from loss given default and exposure at default, because a default with high recovery is a different problem from one with low recovery. It also includes early warning signals, credit migration, and the path from financial distress to formal default, restructuring, or cure. Outputs feed pricing, provisioning, capital planning, and portfolio monitoring, but the models inform decisions rather than make them.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These models run on a data foundation that combines financial statements, payment histories, market prices, credit spreads, ratings, covenant terms, macroeconomic series, and sometimes news or filings. The infrastructure is usually a data warehouse or lakehouse with batch and streaming pipelines, point-in-time feature stores, and model registries that keep training and serving data consistent. Compute may be cloud based or on premises, with Python, SQL, and distributed frameworks such as Spark for large scale feature work. Because defaults are rare events, the platform must handle imbalanced samples, long histories, and strict lineage so that every prediction can be traced back to the data and code that produced it.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts with feature engineering from accounting ratios, leverage and coverage measures, liquidity, payment behavior, market implied signals, and text extracted from filings or news. Common models include logistic regression, survival analysis, gradient boosted trees, and neural networks, with graph methods used to capture contagion or shared exposure across firms. Validation relies on out of time backtests, vintage analysis, and calibration checks, not just ranking metrics such as AUC or KS. Practitioners also examine stability, reason codes, and sensitivity to macroeconomic scenarios, because a model that ranks well but misstates absolute risk can mislead capital and pricing decisions. Human review and expert overlay remain common, especially for large exposures, unusual structures, and names where data is thin.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Data rights and provenance matter because credit models often use licensed market data, private financials, payment records, and alternative sources whose terms may limit reuse or require consent. Teams document where each input came from, how it was transformed, and which model version consumed it, so that an auditor or regulator can reconstruct a decision. Model risk management typically covers independent validation, documentation, ongoing monitoring, drift detection, and controls for bias or fair lending concerns. Risks include overfitting to a benign period, stale or revised data, feedback loops that amplify credit cycles, and the use of proxies that correlate with protected characteristics. Provenance and explainability are not optional extras, they are part of making the output defensible to risk committees, auditors, and supervisors.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward more frequent updates, with monthly or daily monitoring replacing annual scorecard cycles in many portfolios. Alternative data, supply chain links, cyber signals, and climate related exposures are being tested as additional inputs, though their coverage and stability vary. Text and graph models are likely to play a larger role as firms try to connect news, filings, and counterparty networks into earlier warnings. Regulators and internal reviewers are asking for clearer explanations, better calibration, and evidence that models work across cycles, not just in the most recent sample. The direction is toward systems that combine statistical prediction with human judgment, scenario analysis, and transparent documentation rather than a single black box score.
